item.title: Nordic Consumer Culture
item.content:encoded:
The Nordic region exhibits a distinctive consumer culture marked by paradoxes: societies balance egalitarian values with status-consciousness, individualism with collective welfare systems, and modesty with aspiration. The Nordic welfare state uniquely aligns state and individual interests, creating a distinctive marketplace. Despite growing research examining Nordic consumption patterns—from branding and cultural phenomena to alternative food markets and immigrant experiences—significant gaps remain in understanding how these contradictions manifest across consumption practices and market formations.

This special issue seeks to advance comprehensive scholarship on Nordic consumer culture by publishing novel and critically grounded research that explores the interplay between state, market, and consumer practices. The editors welcome contributions analyzing market dynamics, investigating paradoxes inherent in Nordic consumption, and examining how macro-level contexts including welfare policies, cultural myths, and political ideologies shape consumer behavior, with particular interest in innovative methodologies and interdisciplinary approaches.

Appel publié par Qualitative Market Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • State-market-consumer relations and welfare consumption
  • Neoliberalization and privatization of welfare services
  • Nordic imaginaries, myths, and branding
  • Sustainability, nature consumption, and friluftsliv
  • Immigration, minorities, and consumer integration
  • Indigenous consumption and colonial legacies
  • Gender, family, and domestic consumption practices
  • Egalitarianism, conformity, and status distinction
  • Consumer resistance and alternative markets
  • Digitalization and platform consumption
  • Dark consumption, Nordic Noir, and dystopian aesthetics
  • Trust and distrust in state institutions
  • Nordic brands and cultural exports
  • New Nordic movements and manifestos
  • Contradictions in Nordic consumer culture

item.title: Baudrillard's fatal present
item.content:encoded:
Joel Hietanen, University of Helsinki

Søren Askegaard, University of Southern Denmark

Onni Tulensalo, Aalto University School of Business

This special issue seeks to address the significant absence of Baudrillard's social theory from contemporary marketing and consumer research, despite his foundational contributions to understanding consumption as a system of signs rather than need satisfaction. The editors argue that his radical critique of consumer society remains largely neglected or misunderstood within the field, despite being recognized as canonical work and despite contemporary calls to reconsider his insights for understanding current consumer culture.

The issue invites scholarly engagement with Baudrillard's complex theoretical framework, including his concepts of fatal strategies, hyperreality, and the intensification of signification toward implosion. Contributors are encouraged to explore how his work illuminates contemporary consumption phenomena—from sustainability discourse to market inequality—and to investigate whether fatal strategies and accelerationist impulses offer alternative perspectives on capitalist realism and consumer critique.

Appel publié par Consumption Markets & Culture. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Baudrillard's critique of consumer society and consumption as a system of signs
  • Postmodern thought and its applications in marketing and consumer research
  • The concept of fatal strategies and their relevance to contemporary consumer culture
  • Hyperreality, simulation, and the collapse of meaning in consumer markets
  • Sustainability, environmental discourse, and sign proliferation in consumer culture
  • Symbolic exchange and death as critiques of political economy
  • The relationship between subject and object in late capitalism and consumer behavior
  • Critiques of emancipatory consumer narratives and resistive practices
  • The role of excess, spectacle, and implosion in understanding contemporary consumption
  • Applications of Baudrillard's theory beyond marketing, including social sciences broadly

Timeline

  • June 30, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Advertising Narratives: Transportation, Imagination, and Brand Storytelling
item.content:encoded:
Eunjin (Anna) Kim, University of Southern California

Robert Kozinets, University of Southern California

The proliferation of AI tools and digital platforms is transforming advertising storytelling into an adaptive, multi-authored process where narratives are created, circulated, and remixed across humans, algorithms, and channels. This raises critical questions about how stories function as persuasive and cultural resources when they are fragmented, personalized, and constantly recombined by algorithms and influencers. The special issue addresses gaps in understanding what makes advertising narratives compelling in this evolving landscape.

While established psychological mechanisms like transportation, empathy, and identification explain narrative effectiveness, these mechanisms are being tested in environments of short-form content, emerging formats, and AI-generated narratives. Simultaneously, cultural and ethical dimensions remain underexplored—including the role of authenticity, the risks of manipulation, the tension between entertainment and persuasion, and how algorithmic storytelling interacts with human creativity and consumer meaning-making.

Appel publié par International Journal of Advertising. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • (Re-)Conceptualizing advertising storytelling in contemporary contexts

  • Moving beyond 'do narratives work in advertising?' toward 'how do they work in contemporary media environments?'
  • Investigating the craft of advertising storytelling from the creator's perspective
  • Revisiting narrative advertising persuasion mechanisms such as transportation, empathy, identification, and mental simulation in fragmented and multi-platform environments
  • Comparing effectiveness of narrative versus non-narrative advertising approaches
  • Investigating questions about authorship, coherence, authenticity, and credibility when campaigns function as adaptive or transmedia flows
  • Examining how algorithmic and human-authored narratives interact to create or fracture meanings for consumers

  • The role of retro-narratives, nostalgia, and other human and cultural elements in advertising
  • Micro-narratives in TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts: narrative advertising strategies for persuasion in seconds
  • Examining forms, structures, and impacts of influencer storytelling around the globe
  • Cross-device coherence in narrative advertising across TV, mobile, and digital formats
  • Algorithmic sequencing and recombination of story fragments and implications for narrative coherence and persuasion

item.title: The Exotic States of Americana
item.content:encoded:
Alan Bradshaw, Royal Holloway, University of London

Joel Hietanen, University of Helsinki

Marketing and consumer research is extremely American on every level. Though consumer culture varies across the globe, what lies beneath is irreducibly North American. Consumer culture as a phenomenon is an American invention and export. Americana was in unprecedented ascendancy from the 1950s and 1960s, particularly with the neoliberal state apparatus that emerged in the early 1980s Reagan years.

Alternative historicizations exist, such as the Qing Dynasty, the Elizabethan court, and the Industrial Revolution. However, consumerism in its spirit, ideology, mode of subjectivation, seductiveness, excess, imperialism, and globalization is largely understood and experienced throughout the globe as fundamentally Yankee, as intrinsic to the US dollar itself.

Appel publié par Consumption Markets & Culture. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Histories of consumer culture as US soft power
  • Flattery and imitation: the keen attempts to reproduce Americana across the globe
  • American hegemony and the professionally polished field of consumer culture theory
  • Anthropologists, ironically or otherwise, explaining exotic Americana for the benefit of the rest of the world
  • Analyses of contemporary modes of Vassalisation
  • Resistances of all kinds: attempts to counter and break from American consumerism through experiments in commodification and hyper-consumerism
  • Submissions that are polemical, Gonzo, inspired by Baudrillard's America or Adorno's Minima Moralia or Why I Want to Fuck Ronald Reagan that are radical of heart and stylistically break with the norms and expectations branded into doctoral students
